title: VFR Flight Plans — Elements, Filing, Activating, and Closing

questions.text: A pilot completes an ICAO Form 7233-4 VFR flight plan. In Item 19 (Endurance), the pilot writes '0130' — the planned 1 hour 30 minute ETE. In Item 16, the pilot writes '0430' — total fuel on board in hours and minutes. What is the consequence of this entry error?

options.label: A
options.text: The flight plan will be rejected by Leidos Flight Service — automated systems validate that endurance must always exceed ETE by at least 30 minutes for day VFR flights, and 0130 endurance with 0430 ETE fails this automated check

options.label: B
options.text: SAR will search the wrong geographic area — with 0130 endurance (90 minutes of fuel), search teams will calculate the maximum range the aircraft could have flown from departure and focus the search in a radius too small to find an aircraft that actually carried 4.5 hours of fuel

options.label: C
options.text: SAR will believe the aircraft has 1 hour 30 minutes of fuel on board with an ETE of 4 hours 30 minutes — they will calculate the aircraft ran out of fuel approximately 3 hours before reaching the destination and deploy search resources to the wrong area of the route

options.label: D
options.text: No consequence — Flight Service uses Item 16 ETE as the primary search timer and Item 19 endurance as a secondary check; the SAR team will cross-reference both fields and identify the transposition error before initiating any search

questions.explanation: The Endurance field (Item 19) defines the maximum possible SAR search radius by telling SAR how far the aircraft could have flown before fuel exhaustion. If the pilot incorrectly enters ETE (0130 = 90 minutes of flight time) as the endurance instead of actual fuel on board (0430 = 4 hours 30 minutes), SAR teams will calculate a search radius based on only 90 minutes of fuel rather than 4.5 hours. The aircraft could be up to 3 hours further along the route than SAR calculates — dramatically decreasing the probability of finding the aircraft in a survivable timeframe. Option B also describes a consequence but inverts the error: the described result of 'fuel ran out 3 hours before destination' is analytically incorrect — SAR interprets endurance as maximum possible fuel, not a depletion time signature. Option C invents an automated plan validation check that does not exist.

questions.text: A pilot files a VFR flight plan, departs from an uncontrolled airport, and lands at a Class D towered airport. The tower controller says 'Skyhawk 123AB, taxi to parking, clear the runway.' Twenty-five minutes later, FSS initiates a communication search. What did the pilot fail to do?

options.label: A
options.text: Close the VFR flight plan with Flight Service — VFR flight plans are closed exclusively by the pilot contacting FSS directly (via phone or radio); ATC towers close only IFR flight plans; the pilot's failure to close triggered the SAR sequence

options.label: B
options.text: Nothing — the tower controller's landing clearance at a Class D airport constitutes automatic VFR flight plan closure under FAA Order JO 7110.65; the FSS communication search was initiated in error and should be canceled by contacting the TRACON

options.label: C
options.text: Request flight following — if the pilot had requested VFR flight following from TRACON, the radar service would have automatically closed the VFR flight plan upon landing at the Class D airport; the error was not requesting radar service

options.label: D
options.text: Activate the VFR flight plan — a VFR flight plan that is filed but never activated expires 2 hours after the proposed departure time without initiating any SAR procedures; the SAR response suggests the pilot did activate the plan but failed to close it with Flight Service after landing

questions.explanation: This is one of the most common and costly errors in private pilot operations: assuming the tower closes a VFR flight plan. ATC towers DO close IFR flight plans for IFR arrivals — but VFR flight plans are the pilot's exclusive responsibility to close. The tower is not connected to the FSS flight plan tracking system for VFR aircraft. After landing at any airport (towered or not), the pilot must contact FSS directly — by calling 1-800-WX-BRIEF or by radio — to close the VFR flight plan. Failure to close within 30 minutes of ETA triggers the FSS search sequence: QALQ → INREQ → ALNOT → full SAR activation. This wastes significant federal resources and can result in enforcement action. Option A falsely claims ATC landing clearance closes a VFR plan. Option D invents a flight-following-based automatic closure that does not exist.

questions.text: A pilot checks the sectional chart and Chart Supplement for the destination airport, noting the runway is 3,800 feet long and the traffic pattern is standard left traffic for Runway 18. Just before departure, the pilot checks NOTAMs and sees 'RWY 18/36 CLSD. TEMPO. WED-FRI 0700L-1700L.' The flight is planned to arrive Friday at 1530L. What is the correct action?

options.label: A
options.text: Contact ATC for a waiver — VFR pilots may request a temporary waiver from Approach Control to land on a NOTAM-closed runway if no alternate exists within 50 miles; the ARTCC has authority to approve individual VFR landings during maintenance closures

options.label: B
options.text: Proceed — the NOTAM applies to scheduled airline operations only; Part 91 private operations are exempt from TEMPO runway closure NOTAMs because the closures are issued by airport authorities rather than FAA ATC

options.label: C
options.text: Proceed as planned — TEMPO runway closures are advisory only for VFR aircraft; a closed runway designation indicates paving work and pilots may land on the taxiway parallel to the closed runway as an alternate surface if the runway is unavailable

options.label: D
options.text: Identify an alternate airport — landing on a NOTAM-closed runway is prohibited; the pilot must either plan to arrive after 1700L when the closure ends, divert to an alternate airport, or request an exception from the airport manager prior to departure

questions.explanation: A NOTAM with 'RWY 18/36 CLSD TEMPO WED-FRI 0700L-1700L' means the only runway at this airport is closed to ALL aircraft during the stated window. A 1530L Friday arrival falls within the closure period. Landing on a closed runway is a serious safety violation — construction equipment and workers may be on the surface. The correct actions: (1) Delay departure to arrive after 1700L when the closure ends, (2) divert to a different airport, or (3) contact the airport directly to confirm whether an exemption or special arrangement exists. This scenario demonstrates exactly why NOTAMs must be checked as close to departure as possible — the sectional and Chart Supplement showed a functional airport; only the NOTAM revealed the operational hazard. Option A is factually dangerous — landing on a taxiway is not an approved alternate. Options C and D invent ATC waiver authority and Part 91 exemptions that do not exist.

questions.text: During a cross-country, a pilot's EFB shuts down due to thermal overload in direct sunlight. The pilot does not have paper charts or a secondary device. The pilot is approximately 40 miles from the destination over unfamiliar terrain. What is the MOST dangerous aspect of this situation?

options.label: A
options.text: The loss of the weather overlay — without FIS-B weather data from the EFB, the pilot has no way to evaluate developing convection or forecast changes ahead, which is the primary safety function of the EFB in cross-country operations

options.label: B
options.text: The loss of checklist access — modern EFBs store all aircraft emergency and abnormal checklists; without the EFB, the pilot must recall all emergency procedures from memory, which significantly degrades emergency outcome probability in a complex situation

options.label: C
options.text: The loss of all navigational situational awareness — without a backup source of aeronautical chart data and own-ship positioning, the pilot cannot confirm current position, identify nearby airports for emergency diversion, or verify airspace boundaries in unfamiliar terrain

options.label: D
options.text: The loss of ATC communication capability — modern EFBs serve as backup communication systems; without the EFB operational, the pilot must rely on the aircraft's primary radio, which may have reduced capability in mountainous terrain

questions.explanation: The most dangerous consequence of total EFB failure without a backup is the complete loss of navigational situational awareness — the pilot cannot confirm position, identify the nearest airports for diversion, or verify airspace boundaries. In unfamiliar terrain 40 miles from the destination, erroneous dead reckoning could lead to airspace incursions (TFR or Class B floor penetration) or CFIT (Controlled Flight Into Terrain) if terrain MEFs cannot be verified. AC 91-78A addresses this exact risk by requiring a backup navigation strategy. Option A (weather overlay loss) is a significant function but is secondary to the loss of basic navigation data. Option C falsely identifies EFBs as communication systems — EFBs are navigation/information tools and do not replace the aircraft radio. Option D overemphasizes checklist loss as the primary risk when navigational uncertainty is the immediate flight safety priority.

questions.text: A pilot files a VFR flight plan via ForeFlight (EFB) before departing. After takeoff from an uncontrolled airport, the pilot forgets to activate the plan via the EFB. Sixty minutes later, the pilot lands safely at the destination. What is the priority sequence of actions upon landing?

options.label: A
options.text: Immediately call 1-800-WX-BRIEF before shutdown to attempt to both activate and close the plan — explain that the flight is complete; this prevents FSS from interpreting the unactivated plan as a future departure if it is still in the queue approaching the 2-hour expiration

options.label: B
options.text: No action required — an unactivated VFR flight plan automatically expires 2 hours after the proposed departure time with no SAR consequence; since the pilot has already landed safely, the plan will simply fall out of the system without triggering any emergency response

options.label: C
options.text: Contact ATC departure control and ask them to verify plan status — the terminal radar facility that covers the departure airports may have correlated the aircraft radar return with the filed plan and automatically activated it without the pilot's knowledge

options.label: D
options.text: Shutdown the aircraft, log the flight, then call 1-800-WX-BRIEF to close the flight plan — since the plan was never activated, FSS has no active SAR timer for this flight and the call is a courtesy notification

questions.explanation: The correct action is to contact FSS immediately upon landing, even for an unactivated plan. The reason: while an unactivated plan does eventually expire without SAR action, the proposed departure time on the original filed plan is used to calculate the 2-hour expiration window. Depending on the proposed departure time vs. actual departure vs. current time, the situation may be closer to the 2-hour expiration than the pilot realizes. Calling FSS immediately upon landing explains the flight is complete and allows FSS to resolve the plan status cleanly. Option A (shutdown first, then call) risks reaching the 2-hour threshold if the pilot is delayed by post-landing procedures. Option C falsely implies ATC radar facilities automatically activate VFR flight plans — ATC does not manage VFR flight plan activation. Option D correctly describes what happens to an unactivated plan but creates a false sense of security — calling FSS is still best practice to confirm plan disposition.

questions.text: A pilot planning a cross-country notes a Military Operations Area (MOA) along the planned route shown on the sectional chart. How should the pilot determine whether the MOA will be active during the planned flight time?

options.label: A
options.text: Assume the MOA is active at all times and reroute around it — VFR aircraft are prohibited from planning any flight that intersects a MOA boundary regardless of published hours because the military can activate MOAs without advance notice

options.label: B
options.text: Contact the FSS weather briefer — FSS maintains a real-time database of active Special Use Airspace and will advise whether the MOA is hot or cold during the pilot's planned transit time, which constitutes legally sufficient verification

options.label: C
options.text: Check the Sectional Chart legend for the MOA hours of operation — all active MOAs publish their scheduled hot times in the chart legend; the pilot may transit the MOA if the planned flight is outside the published scheduled hours

options.label: D
options.text: Check the Chart Supplement for the MOA's controlling agency and phone number; contact the controlling agency (typically a Military Scheduling office) directly to verify active/inactive status for the planned transit time, or call FSS who can check SUA status

questions.explanation: MOAs are Special Use Airspace where flight activities that may be hazardous to non-participating aircraft occur. The MOA may or may not be active during the planned flight. The Chart Supplement lists each MOA's controlling agency and contact information (typically a military scheduling office with a phone number). The pilot should call this number directly to ask 'Will the [name] MOA be active for flight from [time] to [time] on [date]?' FSS can also confirm SUA status via the 1-800-WX-BRIEF system. If confirmed inactive: the pilot may legally transit the MOA as though it were Class E airspace. If confirmed active: the pilot should route around it. Option A incorrectly identifies the sectional legend as the real-time status source — the legend shows scheduled hours but not real-time activation status. Option B identifies FSS as a valid check (correct), but omits the direct controlling agency contact as an equally valid method. Option D overstates the restriction — VFR pilots may legally transit an inactive MOA.

questions.text: A pilot lands at a towered airport, completing a VFR cross-country. The tower says 'Skyhawk 123AB, contact Ground on 121.7.' The pilot switches to Ground and taxis to parking. On the way to the FBO, a friend calls and the pilot spends 20 minutes on the phone. The pilot then goes inside for lunch. Forty minutes after landing, the pilot's phone rings — it is FSS. What must have happened?

options.label: A
options.text: The tower controller noticed the VFR flight plan on the scope and proactively called FSS to investigate — controllers at Class D airports monitor VFR flight plan status for aircraft under their control and initiate SAR inquiries on behalf of pilots

options.label: B
options.text: The pilot's ADS-B ground track showed the aircraft landed but FSS could see the transponder went silent at the wrong location; the ADS-B position data triggered an automated SAR position mismatch alert sent to the pilot's filed phone number

options.label: C
options.text: The pilot did not close the VFR flight plan with FSS — the tower does not close VFR flight plans; 30+ minutes elapsed past ETA without a pilot-initiated closure, triggering the FSS communication search sequence (QALQ followed by an information request)

options.label: D
options.text: The pilot's EFB auto-activated the flight plan without the pilot's knowledge; the system registered the aircraft as airborne longer than the ETE and automatically sent an alert to FSS, which triggered the search

questions.explanation: The tower ground controller cleared the aircraft to park — nothing more. The tower does not close VFR flight plans. The pilot's responsibility upon landing: immediately call FSS (1-800-WX-BRIEF or by radio) to close the VFR flight plan. The pilot was distracted by a phone call and lunch, allowing 40 minutes to elapse past the ETA. At the 30-minute mark, FSS initiated a QALQ (communication search attempting to reach the pilot by phone and radio) — which is the call the pilot received. Had the pilot not answered, FSS would have escalated to INREQ (Information Request to local facilities) and potentially ALNOT (Alert Notice to SAR). This scenario illustrates why VFR flight plan closing is a legal obligation under 14 CFR 91.153, not an optional courtesy. Options A, C, and D describe ATC and automated system capabilities that do not exist or function as described.
questions.sjt_rationale: The scenario maps directly to a real-world training failure: pilots learn 'file your flight plan' but not the equally critical 'close your flight plan.' The hazardous attitude at work is Complacency — assuming the system will resolve itself. It will not.

questions.text: During a checkride oral, the DPE covers the applicant's EFB with a clipboard and says: 'Your EFB just died. You are here — 15 miles northwest of the TFR you noted in your briefing. Continue.' The applicant freezes and says 'I need my iPad.' What does this demonstrate, and what should the applicant have done?

options.label: A
options.text: Nothing concerning — EFB failure is a theoretical scenario not expected to be managed in real time during an oral examination; the applicant's first priority is to correctly recite the TFR avoidance procedure from memory, after which the DPE will return the EFB for continued navigation

options.label: B
options.text: The demonstration reveals complete dependence on the EFB for basic positional awareness — the applicant failed to maintain independent situational awareness and cannot navigate without GPS own-ship position; the applicant should have produced a paper sectional or secondary device and positively identified their position using pilotage from visible landmarks

options.label: C
options.text: Normal operational response — commercial pilots fly with dual EFB setups and professional standards require a backup system only in Part 121 operations; a private pilot applicant freezing on EFB failure reflects an appropriate awareness of the severity of the problem

options.label: D
options.text: An acceptable limitation — the DPE was creating an unrealistic scenario; no FAA-required competency requires a private pilot to navigate without a functional EFB during a practical test; the applicant may request the EFB be returned so the checkride can continue properly

questions.explanation: The DPE's EFB removal test is a standard, well-documented evaluation technique. An applicant who cannot navigate without the EFB has demonstrated a critical competency gap: they are following a magenta line without understanding where they are. The correct response: (1) produce the paper sectional chart or secondary device that should have been part of the preflight backup strategy; (2) identify a visible landmark (lake, town, highway intersection); (3) correlate that landmark to the sectional chart; (4) confirm position relative to the TFR boundary; (5) continue the briefing. Additionally, knowing where the TFR was from memory (briefed pre-flight) should allow the applicant to state: 'We are northwest of the TFR. We would continue on our planned route that routes south of the boundary.' AC 91-78A requires a backup strategy precisely because this situation can occur in actual flight — an applicant who cannot demonstrate it in the oral cannot be expected to handle it in the air.
questions.sjt_rationale: The freeze response demonstrates over-reliance on technology — the aviation equivalent of a pilot who cannot fly without autopilot. The ACS requires demonstrated proficiency in traditional navigation as a backup regardless of EFB use. Option B is the correct assessment and recovery path.
